name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q01 - Plasma proteins and serum matching

questiontext.text:
Match the blood plasma components in List I with their corresponding functions or descriptions in List II, and select the correct combination.

List I List II
(a) Fibrinogen(i) Osmotic balance
(b) Globulins(ii) Plasma without clotting factors
(c) Albumins(iii) Coagulation of blood
(d) Serum(iv) Defense mechanisms

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood plasma is a straw-coloured viscous fluid containing major proteins—fibrinogen, globulins, and albumins—along with inactive clotting factors.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Fibrinogens are needed for clotting or coagulation of blood, pairing (a) with (iii). Globulins are primarily involved in defense mechanisms of the body, pairing (b) with (iv). Albumins help maintain osmotic balance, pairing (c) with (i). Plasma without the clotting factors is called serum, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q02 - Normal blood counts and haemoglobin levels

questiontext.text:
Match the blood components in List I with their normal reference values in a healthy adult human in List II.

List I List II
(a) Erythrocytes(i) \(6000\text{--}8000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\)
(b) Leucocytes(ii) \(12\text{--}16\ \text{g per }100\ \text{mL}\)
(c) Platelets(iii) \(5\text{--}5.5\ \text{millions mm}^{-3}\)
(d) Haemoglobin(iv) \(1,50,000\text{--}3,50,000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Formed elements constitute nearly 45 per cent of human blood and have characteristic normal concentrations in healthy individuals.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
A healthy adult man has an average of \(5\text{--}5.5\ \text{millions}\) of erythrocytes (RBCs) \(\text{mm}^{-3}\) of blood, pairing (a) with (iii). Leucocytes (WBCs) average \(6000\text{--}8000\ \text{mm}^{-3}\) of blood, pairing (b) with (i). Blood normally contains \(1,50,000\text{--}3,50,000\) platelets \(\text{mm}^{-3}\), pairing (c) with (iv). A healthy individual has \(12\text{--}16\ \text{g}\) of haemoglobin in every \(100\ \text{mL}\) of blood, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q03 - Leucocyte types, abundance, and functions

questiontext.text:
Match the types of white blood cells in List I with their percentage of total WBCs and primary functions in List II.

List I List II
(a) Neutrophils(i) \(0.5\text{--}1\%\); secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin
(b) Basophils(ii) \(20\text{--}25\%\); B and T forms for immune responses
(c) Eosinophils(iii) \(60\text{--}65\%\); phagocytic cells destroying foreign organisms
(d) Lymphocytes(iv) \(2\text{--}3\%\); resist infections and associated with allergic reactions

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Leucocytes are classified into granulocytes (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils) and agranulocytes (lymphocytes, monocytes), each having a distinct proportion and immune role.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Neutrophils are the most abundant WBCs (\(60\text{--}65\%\)) and act as phagocytic cells, pairing (a) with (iii). Basophils are the least abundant (\(0.5\text{--}1\%\)) and secrete histamine, serotonin, and heparin during inflammatory reactions, pairing (b) with (i). Eosinophils constitute \(2\text{--}3\%\) of total WBCs, resist infections, and are associated with allergic reactions, pairing (c) with (iv). Lymphocytes make up \(20\text{--}25\%\) and consist of B and T forms responsible for immune responses, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q04 - ABO blood groups and transfusion compatibility

questiontext.text:
Match the ABO blood groups in List I with their plasma antibodies and donor compatibility in List II.

List I List II
(a) Group A(i) Anti-A in plasma; compatible donors B, O
(b) Group B(ii) Nil antibodies in plasma; universal recipient
(c) Group AB(iii) Anti-A and anti-B in plasma; universal donor
(d) Group O(iv) Anti-B in plasma; compatible donors A, O

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
ABO blood grouping depends on the surface antigens A and B on RBCs and the natural antibodies (anti-A and anti-B) in plasma, which determine safe donor-recipient transfusion matching.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Blood group A carries antigen A on RBCs and anti-B in plasma, so it can receive blood from groups A and O, pairing (a) with (iv). Blood group B carries antigen B on RBCs and anti-A in plasma, so it can receive blood from groups B and O, pairing (b) with (i). Blood group AB has both A and B antigens and nil antibodies in plasma, making these individuals universal recipients, pairing (c) with (ii). Blood group O has nil surface antigens and both anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma, making these individuals universal donors, pairing (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iv), (b)-(i), (c)-(ii), (d)-(iii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q05 - Circulatory patterns across animal groups

questiontext.text:
Match the animal groups in List I with their characteristic circulatory pathway and heart structure in List II.

List I List II
(a) Arthropods and molluscs(i) 3-chambered heart; incomplete double circulation
(b) Fishes(ii) 4-chambered heart; complete double circulation
(c) Amphibians and most reptiles(iii) Open circulatory system with blood sinuses
(d) Crocodiles, birds, and mammals(iv) 2-chambered heart; single circulation

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animal circulatory systems are either open or closed, and vertebrate hearts show evolutionary progression from 2-chambered single circulation to 4-chambered complete double circulation.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Arthropods and molluscs possess an open circulatory system in which blood enters open cavities called sinuses, pairing (a) with (iii). Fishes have a 2-chambered heart (one atrium and one ventricle) and exhibit single circulation, pairing (b) with (iv). Amphibians and reptiles (except crocodiles) have a 3-chambered heart (two atria and a single ventricle) where oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix, showing incomplete double circulation, pairing (c) with (i). Crocodiles, birds, and mammals have a 4-chambered heart with two atria and two ventricles, maintaining complete double circulation, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q06 - Valves and septa of the human heart

questiontext.text:
Match the structural features of the human heart in List I with their anatomical locations in List II.

List I List II
(a) Tricuspid valve(i) Guards opening between left atrium and left ventricle
(b) Bicuspid (mitral) valve(ii) Thick-walled partition separating left and right ventricles
(c) Semilunar valves(iii) Guards opening between right atrium and right ventricle
(d) Inter-ventricular septum(iv) Guard openings of ventricles into pulmonary artery and aorta

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The four chambers of the human heart are separated by muscular and fibrous septa, and unidirectional blood flow is maintained by atrioventricular and semilunar valves.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
The tricuspid valve (three muscular flaps) guards the opening between the right atrium and right ventricle, pairing (a) with (iii). The bicuspid or mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle, pairing (b) with (i). Semilunar valves guard the openings of the right and left ventricles into the pulmonary artery and aorta respectively, pairing (c) with (iv). The thick-walled inter-ventricular septum separates the left and right ventricles, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q07 - ECG waves and cardiac cycle events

questiontext.text:
Match the electrocardiographic waves and heart sounds in List I with the corresponding physiological events during a cardiac cycle in List II.

List I List II
(a) P-wave(i) Ventricular depolarisation initiating ventricular systole
(b) QRS complex(ii) Closure of tricuspid and bicuspid valves
(c) T-wave(iii) Atrial depolarisation leading to atrial contraction
(d) First heart sound (lub)(iv) Ventricular repolarisation marking the end of systole

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An ECG records the electrical activity of the heart during each cardiac cycle, while mechanical valve closures produce characteristic heart sounds.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
The P-wave represents electrical excitation (depolarisation) of the atria, which leads to contraction of both atria, pairing (a) with (iii). The QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles, initiating ventricular systole, pairing (b) with (i). The T-wave represents the return of ventricles from the excited state to normal (repolarisation), with its end marking the end of systole, pairing (c) with (iv). The first heart sound (lub) is produced by the closure of the tricuspid and bicuspid valves at the onset of ventricular systole, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q08 - Blood vessel layers and autonomic cardiac regulation

questiontext.text:
Match the vascular layers and autonomic neural pathways in List I with their structural or regulatory descriptions in List II.

List I List II
(a) Tunica intima(i) Smooth muscle and elastic fibres; comparatively thin in veins
(b) Tunica media(ii) Decreases heart rate and speed of action potential conduction
(c) Sympathetic neural signals(iii) Inner lining of squamous endothelium in arteries and veins
(d) Parasympathetic neural signals(iv) Increases heart rate and strength of ventricular contraction

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Arteries and veins share a three-layered wall (tunica intima, tunica media, tunica externa), while cardiac output is moderated by the medulla oblongata via sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Tunica intima is the inner lining of squamous endothelium in blood vessels, pairing (a) with (iii). Tunica media is the middle layer of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, which is comparatively thin in veins, pairing (b) with (i). Sympathetic neural signals increase the rate of heart beat, strength of ventricular contraction, and cardiac output, pairing (c) with (iv). Parasympathetic neural signals decrease the heart rate, speed of conduction of action potential, and cardiac output, pairing (d) with (ii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(iii), (b)-(i), (c)-(iv), (d)-(ii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_MATCH_Q09 - Disorders of the human circulatory system

questiontext.text:
Match the circulatory disorders in List I with their clinical characteristics in List II.

List I List II
(a) Hypertension(i) Acute chest pain due to insufficient oxygen reaching heart muscle
(b) Coronary Artery Disease (CAD)(ii) Repeated blood pressure readings of \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher
(c) Angina pectoris(iii) Heart unable to pump blood effectively; lung congestion
(d) Heart failure(iv) Arterial lumen narrowed by calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissue

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Disorders of the circulatory system arise from elevated arterial pressure, atherosclerotic narrowing of coronary vessels, myocardial hypoxia, or impaired pumping efficiency.

Step 2: Concept-by-Concept Pairing
Hypertension (high blood pressure) is diagnosed when repeated blood pressure checks are \(140/90\ \text{mm Hg}\) or higher (above the normal \(120/80\ \text{mm Hg}\)), pairing (a) with (ii). Coronary Artery Disease (atherosclerosis) narrows the lumen of arteries supplying the heart muscle due to deposits of calcium, fat, cholesterol, and fibrous tissues, pairing (b) with (iv). Angina pectoris is a symptom of acute chest pain when not enough oxygen reaches the heart muscle, pairing (c) with (i). Heart failure occurs when the heart does not pump blood effectively enough to meet the body's needs, often causing congestion of the lungs, pairing (d) with (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct matching is (a)-(ii), (b)-(iv), (c)-(i), (d)-(iii).
